items.note: Padmagupta's Navasāhasāṅka-carita account: a hero sprang from Vasiṣṭha's fire, was named Paramāra ('Slayer of the Enemy') and made supreme ruler; the family originated from him.
The poet Padmagupta was contemporary of Vākpati-Muñja (972-995) and Sindhurāja, author of the Nava-sāhasāṅka-carita.
'The Udayapur prasasti of the reign of Udayāditya (about 1072 A.D.) is the earliest known inscription of the main family of Dhārā to register the mythical birth of the founder.'

claim.value: reign of Udayāditya, about 1072 A.D.; earliest main-line record of fire-birth myth

items.note: Bards differ on fire-origin, but 'none of the dynastic inscriptions of any of these families except those of the Paramāras speaks of their fire-origin'.
Continues the Udayapur prasasti verse: Viśvāmitra took Vasiṣṭha's cow, a hero arose from the fire-pit and was named 'Paramāra'.
Ganguly: 'Paramāra' was not the name of a race but of a family, called Paramāravaṃśa after the hero.
Compares Paramāra naming with Gupta and Pratihāra family names; 'Paramāra' not found in early literature as a race or caste.
Harsola record of Siyaka II, V.S. 1005 = 948 A.D., 'the earliest known record of the dynasty'.
Ganguly judges Gurjara-origin arguments rest on tradition: 'No authentic material has yet been discovered to prove a Gurjara origin of the Paramāras.'
English summary of the Harsola grant naming Vappaiyarāja, Vairisimha and Siyaka.
Other families do not assert fire-origin; grouping under 'Agnikula' called 'a figment of imagination of the bards of the later ages'.
Ganguly argues Rāṣṭrakūṭa origin of the Paramāras from the Harsola grant and Muñja's Rāṣṭrakūṭa titles.
Original home placed in the Deccan; Ā'in-i-Akbarī says Dhanji moved from the Deccan to Mālava.
Padmagupta's Nava-sāhasāṅka-carita (996-1000 A.D.) is the earliest record to call the family 'Paramāra'; earlier grants do not.

items.note: Ganguly's view: Pratihāra rule in Mālava was overthrown and Mālava 'governed by a subordinate chief of the imperial Rāṣṭrakūṭas'.
Between 808 and 812 A.D. Pratihāras expelled from Mālava; new ruler probably Upendra-Kṛṣṇarāja, founder of the Paramāra dynasty.
'The Udayapur prasasti tells us that he "gained the high honour of kingship by his valour."' (of Upendra).
Muñja ascended between 971 and 972; with 25 years per reign Upendra's accession falls in the first quarter of the 9th century.
Banswara (Vāgaḍa) Paramāra family is a collateral branch of the main house of Dhārā, settled mid-9th century.
Muñja's Ujjain plate names Kṛṣṇarāja as earliest ruler, identified with Upendra; Ganguly equates Kanhāda with Kṛṣṇarāja.
Ganguly: Mount Abu as original home rests on tradition; 'very little importance should be attached to this mythical story'.
Suggests Candana and Dūsala were posted at Jalor and Bhinmal as viceroys of the imperial house of Dhārā.
